draft.title: Ethics of biotechnology
card: Ethics asks what is right and wrong. Biotechnology shows what can be done. Ethics asks whether it should be done, and under what rules.
Safety
Could a product or organism harm people, other species or the environment? Testing and regulation aim to manage these risks.
Fairness
Who gets the benefits and who bears the costs? A treatment that only wealthy people can afford raises a question of fairness.
Ownership and nature

Can a company patent a gene? Some say patents reward research, others say genes should not be owned. Some people also object to changing nature itself. Groups weigh these questions differently, so they can reach different views.
draft.remember: Ethical questions about biotechnology have no single answer, because groups weigh the concerns differently.

a.q: Which of these is an ethical question about biotechnology?
opts: Should a company be allowed to patent a human gene?
Which enzyme cuts DNA at a set sequence?
How many bases are in a gene for insulin?
Which microbes turn milk into cheese?
a.why: Whether genes should be owned is a question of right and wrong, so it is about ethics. The other three ask for facts that science can answer without a value judgement.
a.clue: Look for the question about what should be allowed, not what is true.

b.q: A company develops a gene therapy that works well but costs a very large sum per patient. Which ethical concern does this mainly raise?
opts: Fairness, because only some patients may afford it
Safety, because the therapy is known to harm patients
Ownership, because the therapy changes a patient's genes
Changing nature, because the therapy works too well
b.why: The main problem is who can get the treatment, which is fairness. Safety would be the concern if the therapy was risky, but the case says it works well. The cost is not a question of who owns genes.
b.clue: Ask who benefits and who is left out.

a.best: Should a company be allowed to patent a human gene?

b.best: Fairness, because only some patients may afford it

problems.detail: The remember line says ethical questions 'have no single answer', which is more absolute than the card. The card only says groups 'can reach different views'.

Why (b) rules out safety because the therapy 'works well'. A treatment that works can still carry risks, so this reasoning could teach students that working well means safe. The safety option is wrong because the case does not say the therapy harms anyone.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The remember line slightly overstates the card ('no single answer' versus 'can reach different views'), and why (b) wrongly suggests that a treatment that works well must be safe.
